units.text: Perceived Productivity and Measured Productivity

When you watch hundreds of lines appear on the screen, it is hard not to feel acceleration. But the speed at which material appears is not the same as the speed at which you obtain an acceptable result. A workshop can produce more parts and fewer products that pass quality control.
On the other hand, dismissing all gains as illusion would be just as unjustified. Research offers different results precisely because tasks, people, tools, and criteria differ.
Two Experiments, Not an Eternal Verdict

In the controlled experiment reported by Peng and colleagues in 2023, programmers with access to GitHub Copilot completed a task implementing an HTTP server in JavaScript 55.8% faster than the group without access. This is evidence for the task and conditions studied, not a guaranteed reduction in the duration of every software project. [20]

In METR’s study from early 2025, 16 experienced developers worked on 246 tasks in familiar open-source projects. Access to the evaluated tools increased completion time by 19%, while participants later estimated that AI had sped them up. The result concerns a particular context, a small group, and the tools of that period. It does not demonstrate that experts are always slowed down or that assisted programming cannot bring benefits. [19]

The two results do not cancel each other out. A well-bounded task started from scratch and a change in a mature system can have very different distributions of costs. In the latter case, understanding local conventions, integration, and compatibility checks may matter more than producing code text.
What the 2026 Research Adds

A preliminary meta-analysis by Maier and colleagues, published in May 2026, brings together 23 studies with 27 effect estimates. It reports a moderate positive average effect on productivity, but substantial heterogeneity and larger gains in controlled experiments than in some real-world contexts. The effect on learning was not statistically significant. The standardized effect size g = 0.33 for productivity does not mean “33% more productive.” The absence of significance for learning does not demonstrate the absence of every educational effect. [21]

In February 2026, METR explained why it was changing its experimental design: the developers and tasks accepted into the study had become more selective, and simultaneous agent use complicated time measurement. The authors considered larger gains than in the first study plausible, but regarded the new data as weak for precisely estimating their magnitude. Presenting only the negative figure from 2025 as the current verdict would ignore this update. [22]

In a separate survey published in May 2026, METR asked 349 technical workers about the value of assisted work. Reported median estimates indicated increases of 1.4–2 times, depending on the measure. The authors stress that these are counterfactual self-assessments, not independently measured causal results, and discuss reasons for skepticism about the magnitude. The survey informs us about participants’ experiences and expectations; it does not certify a multiplication of value in every organization. [23]
Five Questions Hidden in One Word

When someone says “I am more productive,” they may mean they finish the same task faster. Or produce a better result in the same time. Or work on tasks they would not previously have started. Or produce more by working more hours. Or simply that the activity feels easier and more enjoyable.

All can matter, but they are not the same quantity. An organization must decide what it is trying to improve before celebrating a percentage. A METR analysis of task substitution explicitly raises the difference between accelerating existing work and changing the portfolio of work. [42]

In research by Chen and colleagues at BNY Mellon, based on 2,989 responses and 11 interviews, productivity is treated multidimensionally, beyond the number of commits. The paper, consulted in its arXiv version, helps explain perceptions, competence, and ownership of work; it is not an experiment isolating AI’s effect on the entire firm. [28]
A Better Calculation Than a Slogan

Suppose a task required four hours of implementation and six of verification, integration, and documentation. If AI reduces implementation to one hour and the rest remains unchanged, the total falls from ten to seven hours. Implementation is four times faster; the complete task is not four times faster. The saving is 30%. This is an arithmetic example, not an observed result.

If verification increases, the gain can shrink. If AI also helps with verification, it can grow. If the final result is higher quality, simply comparing hours does not exhaust the benefit. This very flexibility requires measurement rather than choosing the example we like.

An honest evaluation records total time, accepted quality, errors that appear later, and costs transferred to other people. Not merely the speed of the first demonstration. Instead of asking whether AI “is productive,” we can ask what combination of task, person, and process produces a real gain, for whom, and at what cost.
